items.title: 2.10 Electronic configuration and the formation of semiconductors

source_refs.note: Topic 2.10, printed pages 41-42: semiconductors and doping (Figure 2.17).

blocks.text: Semiconductors are materials that conduct electricity under some conditions; they are used in many electronic devices, including smartphones, laptops and cars. Silicon, germanium and arsenic are elements that can act as semiconductors, and semiconductors can be made because of the unique electronic configuration of these elements. Silicon (Z = 14) has the configuration 2, 8, 4, so four electrons in its valence shell. In the pure crystalline form each silicon atom is bonded to four other silicon atoms, and in this form there is no possibility of electronic conduction through the crystal.

blocks.alt: A crystal of pure silicon: nine Si atoms in a square pattern, each joined to four neighbours by covalent bonds drawn as lens shapes holding two electrons, one from each atom; bonds also run out of the edges. Labels: Covalent bond, Silicon valence electrons, Silicon atoms.
blocks.caption: Figure 2.17: A crystal of pure silicon (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 2.17).

blocks.text: P-type and N-type semiconductors are formed by doping a pure semiconductor with impurity atoms. Adding trivalent impurities such as boron or aluminium creates a P-type semiconductor, while adding pentavalent impurities such as phosphorus or arsenic creates an N-type. The difference lies in whether the impurity creates holes, positive charge carriers, in the lattice (P-type) or extra electrons, negative charge carriers (N-type).
